analysis.one_liner: Bans accounting firms from selling consulting services to companies they audit.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Enron collapse, auditors were often the same firms paid millions by their clients for consulting work — meaning a company could hire its own watchdog. This bill would have barred an accounting firm from providing management consulting or other non-audit services to any company it audits, and ordered the Securities and Exchange Commission to write detailed rules within 90 days. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and workers who rely on honest audits — including employees whose retirement savings are tied up in their employer's stock. An independent auditor is more likely to flag accounting problems before a collapse, as critics said happened at Enron, where the same firm earned large fees for both auditing and consulting. Honest companies would also benefit from audits investors can trust.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Investors and workers relying on honest audits

how_it_helps.text: Bars an audit firm from providing management consulting, information technology, organizational, marketing, or business strategy services to its own audit client during the year of the audit.
Requires the SEC to write final rules within 90 days defining prohibited consulting services and identifying other non-audit services that would impair auditor independence.
Declares in findings that an auditor is not independent when it audits its own work, acts as a consultant or advocate for the client, or shares the client's interests.

analysis.who_pays: The large accounting firms, which in that era earned a large share of their revenue selling consulting and technology services to their own audit clients. Corporate clients that liked bundling audit and consulting with one firm would lose that convenience and might pay separate providers.

drawbacks.text: The ban is broad: it prohibits all consulting to audit clients, not just services that clearly create a conflict, which could raise compliance costs for companies and push some audit work to fewer, audit-only firms.
The bill does not address other audit-quality problems — such as who hires and pays the auditor — so it targets one conflict while leaving the basic structure of client-paid audits in place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — an auditor that does not audit its own firm's consulting work — directly serves investors and workers who depend on honest financial statements. The cost falls on accounting firms' consulting revenue and on corporate convenience, not on most ordinary people. The main limitation is that it addresses one conflict-of-interest channel, not the whole audit incentive problem.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Banking Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Boxer introduced the bill on January 24, 2002, weeks after Enron's collapse drew attention to the fact that its auditor also earned large fees for consulting work.
The Senate referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day; no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill attracted no cosponsors during the roughly eleven months it was pending.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee.

Later in the same year, Congress did enact auditor-independence restrictions through separate legislation (the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002), which banned most non-audit services for audit clients — a widely known law, though not among the provided sources.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, the large accounting firms kept the ability to sell consulting services to their own audit clients, since this bill died without any action. Investors and workers gained only indirectly, months later, when a different bill with similar restrictions became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big accounting firms, at least until later reform

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Auditor Independence Act and spoke for it on the Senate floor; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Paul Sarbanes (D-MD)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died there.

against.name: Large accounting firms (the 'Big Five')
against.what_they_did: Widely reported at the time to be lobbying against strict bans on selling consulting services to audit clients, which threatened a major revenue stream; this influence does not appear in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors of either party, so its partisan shape cannot be measured; the committee that buried it was run by the sponsor's own party.

industries.industry: Large accounting firms (the Big Five: Andersen, Deloitte, Ernst & Young, KPMG, PricewaterhouseCoopers)
industries.note: These firms earned substantial revenue selling consulting and technology services to the very companies they audited, and the bill would end that dual role. Their interest in keeping that revenue ran against investors who depend on independent audits.

industries.industry: Management consulting and information technology services
industries.note: Audit clients could no longer buy IT or strategy consulting bundled with their audit, so some of that work would shift to independent consultancies — a gain for standalone consultants, a loss for firms serving audit clients.
Companies would have to procure audit and consulting from different firms and might pay more, but would benefit in credibility with investors from a cleaner audit.
